html:
The Indian Rebellion was a great rising against the rule of the East India Company that began on 10 May 1857, when Indian soldiers, called sepoys, mutinied at Meerut near Delhi. It spread across north and central India and took over a year to put down.

The spark was a rumour that cartridges for the new Enfield rifle were greased with cow and pig fat, offensive to Hindus and Muslims. Deeper grievances lay behind it: annexations of states such as Awadh and Jhansi, new taxes, fear of forced conversion, and princes and landlords pushed aside.

The rebels marched to Delhi and declared the old Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, their leader. Fighting centred on:

  • Delhi, retaken by the British in September 1857.
  • Kanpur, where Nana Sahib rose and British captives were massacred.
  • Lucknow, where the British residency held out under siege.
  • Central India, where Rani Lakshmibai fought.

Both sides killed civilians, and British reprisals were savage. Afterward Parliament ended Company rule. India passed to the Crown under Queen Victoria, the start of the British Raj. Zafar was exiled to Burma, and the Mughal line ended.
